root_causes.description: Badge award evaluation (catalog seeding plus eligibility and per-badge existence checks) is executed synchronously on every badge read instead of when course completion occurs.
Notification list issues two extra counts per request, and the unread count filters on a field not covered by the index that contains isDeleted.

findings.problem: Every badge read (user badges, public badge catalog, user profile) first runs the full award evaluation, which re-seeds the catalog with 5 upserts, reloads and populates all completed course progress, loads all badges and does a per-badge existence query, all of which is write-path work that mostly changes nothing.
findings.performance_principle: Do work when its inputs change, not on every read; do not repeat idempotent setup per request; avoid per-item round trips when one set-based query can answer.

evidence.statement: getUserBadges awaits checkAndAwardBadges before the read query.
checkAndAwardBadges starts with seedDefaultBadges, which loops over DEFAULT_BADGES doing one findOneAndUpdate upsert each, awaited serially.
getAllBadges, a public unauthenticated route, also runs the 5 serial upserts on each call.
All completed CourseProgress documents for the user are loaded in full (including the lessonsCompleted array) and populated with course, then only a count and a category tally are used.
For each eligible badge a separate UserBadge.findOne is awaited inside the loop, and a first award adds create and findById+populate.
The user profile endpoint calls getUserBadges, so a profile view triggers the evaluation; the public route GET /badges/user/:userId needs no authentication.
Derived: 5 default badges give at most 5 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 15 round trips per steady-state badge read, versus 2 needed to read UserBadge with its badge populated.
No runtime evidence (profile, slow-query log, trace) was supplied or found in the repository.

findings.conditions: Matters when badge or profile endpoints are called often (page loads, polling, or crawling of the unauthenticated /badges/user/:userId route) and users hold several completed courses and badges. Assumes only the 5 default badges exist; custom badges add one round trip each. Request rate is unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: Queries use indexed fields (UserBadge unique user+badge, CourseProgress unique user+course, Badge unique slug) so each round trip is cheap and no collection scan was found.
Badge catalog size is fixed at 5 defaults in code, so per-request work is bounded unless custom badges exist.
Searched for caching or a memoised seed flag around the seed and award calls and found none.

Searched for award hooks at course completion (callers of checkAndAwardBadges); only HTTP controllers and the user profile call it, so no existing award-on-completion path makes the read-time check redundant.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Each statement is indexed and the badge catalog is five items, so per-call cost is a small constant of fast queries; if badge reads are infrequent this will never show up against the rest of the database load.
findings.recommendation: Separate awarding from reading. Seed the catalog once at startup or in a migration rather than per request. Make getUserBadges and getAllBadges pure reads. Run the award evaluation when a course reaches completion (or on the explicit POST /badges/evaluate), and inside it replace the per-badge findOne loop with one UserBadge.find for the user's existing badge ids, then one insertMany of the missing ones, using a lean, projected CourseProgress query (select course, no lessonsCompleted) or an aggregation that returns the count and per-category counts.

alternatives.option: Move evaluation to the course-completion event and make reads pure
alternatives.why: Removes the work instead of making it cheaper; reads drop to the minimum two queries.

alternatives.option: Keep evaluation on read but seed once at startup and batch the existence checks and queries
alternatives.why: Cuts round trips to roughly 5 but still does write-path work on every read and on a public route.

alternatives.option: Cache the evaluation result per user for a short time
alternatives.why: Masks the work, adds staleness (a user could miss a badge just earned) and invalidation rules for no gain over doing it on completion.

findings.trade_offs: Awarding on completion needs a hook in the progress-update code and a backfill for users whose completions pre-date it; badge display after a missed event relies on the manual evaluate endpoint. Startup seeding adds a boot-time dependency on the database.

validation.metric: MongoDB commands issued per GET /api/v1/badges/my-badges and per GET user profile request
validation.expectation: Direction: fewer database round trips per read; derived from the code the minimum is 2 (UserBadge.find plus populate) versus up to 15 today, assuming only default badges.
validation.falsifier: If a command-count capture of a staging request shows far fewer than the derived round trips, or badge endpoints are almost never called, the finding does not matter.
validation.guard: A test that asserts getUserBadges issues no write operations and a bounded query count.

commands.command: db.setProfilingLevel(2) on a staging database, call the endpoint once, then db.system.profile.find({ ns: /userbadges|badges|courseprogresses/ }).count()
commands.purpose: Count commands per request in staging to compare with the derived 15.

findings.problem: The notification list runs, serially after the page query, a total count and an unread count; the unread count filters on isRead with recipient and isDeleted, a combination no single index covers, so it must fetch documents to apply the remaining predicate.
findings.performance_principle: Work per request should not grow with the size of the user's whole history when only one page is returned; keep filters answerable from one index.

evidence.statement: Two countDocuments calls are awaited sequentially after the page query, in addition to up to three populate lookups on the page.
Indexes are recipient+createdAt, recipient+isRead, recipient+isDeleted and recipient+isDeleted+createdAt; none holds recipient, isRead and isDeleted together.
No TTL index or scheduled cleanup was found; the repository hard-delete helper is described as manual cleanup.

findings.conditions: Only matters for recipients holding thousands of notifications or more with the list polled or loaded on every page; volumes per user are unknown and assumed to grow without bound because no cleanup was found.

counter_evidence.statement: The page query itself is well indexed (recipient+isDeleted+createdAt matches filter and sort) and limit is capped at 100, so the row transfer is bounded.
Counts use index prefixes on recipient so scan size is limited to one user's notifications, not the collection.
Searched for an N+1 pattern in the list path; populate batches per path so only 3 extra queries run regardless of page size.

findings.recommendation: Measure first. If the unread count shows up in slow-query output, add an index on recipient, isDeleted, isRead and, if counts remain costly for very large histories, run the two counts concurrently (Promise.all) or maintain a per-user unread counter. Otherwise take no action.
findings.trade_offs: A new index costs write amplification on every notification insert and extra memory; a counter adds consistency risk with read, delete and bulk operations.

validation.metric: docsExamined versus nReturned for the unread-count query
validation.expectation: If docsExamined is much larger than the count, the extra index would reduce it; direction only, no magnitude is derivable.
validation.falsifier: docsExamined close to the count, or the query absent from the slow-query log, means no change is warranted.

commands.purpose: Compare docsExamined with returned count for a heavy user.
